column15: Mayor Eric Adams introduced the city's first-ever climate budgeting publication through the city's Fiscal Year (FY) 2025 Executive Budget. column19: •The Essex Pension Fund - for which ECC is the administering authority - recognises both its responsibility to be a trusted investor and the range of potential long-term risks associated with climate change that the Fund, as a long-term investor, faces. The Investment Steering Committee has appointed specialist external managers to a range of investment mandates. The financial impact of issues, including climate change, forms one part of the process that determines the investments made on the Fund's behalf. The Committee continues to review its Responsible Investment (RI) Policy and RI Beliefs - which includes climate change - to ensure that the Fund's mandates are aligned and have an aspiration to be net zero by 2050. As a result, the Fund recently, in collaboration with its Index Tracking Manager, launched a new Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) global Equity Sustainable Transition Fund and has made a £100 million commitment to the Stafford Carbon Offset Opportunity Fund. In addition, the Committee has agreed a set of Climate Change Metrics in line with the Taskforce on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) regulations. \n•The Essex Renewal Fund supports land and property projects in Essex and the investment principles include a commitment to net zero and climate resilience. The fund is part of our commitment to good jobs, future growth and investment, green growth and levelling up the economy. Over the next 20 years, the fund aims to invest over £100m, (subject to affordability) supporting 1,500 jobs and bringing to market enough land to deliver 1,000 new homes.\n

column15: The City's General City Budget consists of special funds and the general fund. Special funds have restrictions on their use while the general fund is made of City revenue without specific restrictions. The general fund makes up about 62% of the City's budget while special funds represent about 38%. The City invests a portion of its budget to sustainability and climate programs and initiatives. However, the City does not currently set aside a specific percentage of its General City Budget towards climate investments. Starting in 2022, the City began identifying investments in green infrastructure with a notation in the City's budget. This is the Capital and Technology Improvement Expenditure Program beginning on the page marked 813 on https://cao.lacity.gov/budget24-25/2024-25%20White%20Book%20-%20Volume%202.pdf#page=339 . The City also actively applies to and receives state and federal funding for climate related projects. Of particular note is the State's Transformative Climate Communities (TCC) Grant. Through the State's TCC program, three L.A. neighborhoods - Watts, Pacoima-Sun Valley, and South L.A. - received awards totaling over $55 million by the State and leveraged over $200 million from the City and partners for projects ranging from affordable housing to rooftop solar and workforce development.

column19: The Los Angeles City Employees' Retirement System (LACERS) provides retirement benefits to the civilian employees of the City, representing 3/5th of the City's workforce. The remaining 2/5th of the workforce has retirement benefits through the Water and Power Employees Retirement Plan (WPERP) or the Los Angeles Fire and Police Pensions (LAFPP). The investment decisions for all three retirement and pension systems are driven by investment policies adopted by each of their respective Boards. LACERS, through its Responsible Investment Policy, Proxy Voting Policy, and ESG Risk Framework, incorporates Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors into its decision-making process. In April 2019, the LACERS Board of Administration approved becoming a signatory of the U.N. Principles for Responsible Investment, which was granted in September 2019. LACERS staff seeks Board approval of its updated annual PRI Action Plan and ESG Risk Framework Action Plan. The Board's investment staff oversee implementation and enforcement of investment policies, which includes managing the investment process beginning with a periodic (currently triennial) asset allocation study. This exercise leads to modifications to the asset allocation structure and policy weightings, setting investment risk budgets, hiring and termination of fund managers, and periodic rebalancing adjustments. LAFPP is currently re-assessing its existing ESG and Proxy Voting Policies to better incorporate ESG into the decision-making process. However, the current Proxy Voting Policy has been the primary tool to assist in pursuing certain policy objectives of which ESG is included. The Board pursues a long-term investment horizon and uses an asset allocation plan that encompasses a strategic, long-term perspective of the capital markets. Sustainable investing goals are paramount to the stability of the Fund over the long-term investment horizon.

The City is exploring and using a wide variety of financing tools for projects, particularly bonds and federal grants. Additional projects are being funded by loan programs, including WIFIA, and operating budgets. The City is also leveraging innovative local financing mechanisms such as the Municipal Investment Fund, which mobilizes private capital to advance climate resilience, energy efficiency, and sustainable infrastructure.

In addition, the City will soon bring forward a bond sale proposition that includes dedicated funding for critical priorities such as drainage improvements, resilience hubs, and complete streets. Together, these investments will expand the City's capacity to address both immediate infrastructure needs and long-term resilience goals.

To maximize federal opportunities, the City has created an IIJA Task Force, housed in the Office of Resilience & Sustainability, to pursue all resilience-related funding opportunities from the IIJA and other federal and state funding streams. Since its inception, the Task Force has secured 16 discretionary grant awards for the City from IIJA and Inflation Reduction Act programs, totaling $157 million. More information here:

Portland has always used it's own funding to support climate planning and action activities, with the addition of occasional grant funding. 

More recently, the City has established a fund to invest in climate-related projects citywide. The Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits fund (PCEF) was passed by 65% of Portland voters in November 2018. It provides a consistent, long-term funding source and oversight structure to ensure that our community's climate action efforts are implemented to support social, economic and environmental benefits for all Portlanders, particularly communities of color and people with low incomes. PCEF's current Climate Investment Plan provides a framework to invest $750 million in community-led clean energy projects and climate solutions like energy-efficient upgrades to make apartment buildings safer and more comfortable during extreme heat, and tree planting to increase shade in neighborhoods that lack tree canopy coverage. The full funding allocation can be found here:

The City has three main tools to effect change — advocacy, regulation, and investment — and we rely on all three to pursue the Council-approved targets. Our targets cannot be achieved with a business as-usual approach. 

Staff's approach has been to prioritize the City's regulatory and advocacy tools over direct City investment in cases where they are more appropriate and effective in delivering intended outcomes. In some cases, City investment is needed upfront to develop, implement and incentivize regulation adoption to drive significant city-wide GHG reductions at a relatively low ongoing cost to the City. Big Move 4 is an example of this: Upfront investment in training, incentives and capacity-building will enable a successful regulation for existing building emissions beginning in 2025. Similarly, City investment in electric vehicle charging infrastructure now will support a faster transition to electric vehicles. 

Staff work closely with Federation of Canadian Municipalities, Union of BC Municipalities, Vancouver Economic Commission, community partners and stakeholders to advocate for dedicated and sustainable funding from senior governments to advance climate investment. 

Through the latest four-year Capital Plan process, Council approved additional funds to augment priority actions, and staff has further identified opportunities to leverage senior government funding and other partnerships, wherever possible. An annual Climate Budget report to Council helps highlight climate-related investment levels and priority unfunded needs to help inform decision-making.

The City's regular debenture program, as well as a mature LVC system involving developer contributions on rezonings, etc., enables funding of long-term capital programs, including those with climate benefits. Debt-funded projects with primary climate focus are identified and funded through our Sustainable Debenture Program, guided by an ICMA-consistent Sustainability Bond Framework. 

The City also participates in the British Columbia Low-Carbon Fuel Standards program, a saleable credit-generating program with proceeds going into a fund for reinvestment into climate-related projects.

column19: In 2017, our CFO signed an Accounting for Sustainability (A4S) statement, supporting climate-related financial disclosure and committing the City to “affirm our commitment to support the voluntary recommendations” of the Taskforce for Climate-related Financial Disclosure (TCFD). Starting in 2018, the City began including unaudited climate-related financial disclosures in its annual financial report. Recommended disclosure includes four core elements: governance, strategy, risk management and metrics and targets. Although support for the TCFD reporting framework is growing, disclosure standards are still evolving out of this voluntary guidance. In November 2021, the International Financial Reporting Standards Foundation (IFRS) announced the formation of an International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) and published prototype climate and general disclosure requirements developed by the Technical Readiness Working Group (TRWG), a group formed by the IFRS Foundation Trustees to undertake preparatory work for the ISSB. Based on TCFD recommendations, this Climate-Related Disclosures Prototype includes more specific disclosures. The formation of the ISSB also includes the commitment from three other organization with similar global reporting framework initiatives to consolidate with the ISSB. Along with these developments, financial regulators and governments across the globe (including Canada) are moving towards mandatory TCFD-type reporting. The City is supportive of these developments in climate-related reporting guidance. For the purposes of this year's report, we have taken into consideration both the TCFD recommendations and the TRWG prototype disclosures. 2024 TCFD disclosure for Vancouver is available here: https://vancouver.ca/files/cov/2024-annual-financial-report.pdf

Glasgow has embarked on a process to establish the correct Model for Climate Investment to formulate a route for delivery and to create a method to allow the private sector to invest in climate related projects supporting the ambitions to become a net zero city. To address barriers and understand the best model for Glasgow, the City Administration Committee approved (21st March 2024) a project budget of £4m to create an internal team and supplement the knowledge and experience with external specialists to establish Glasgow's Model for Climate Investment. Glasgow is specifically focusing on two workstreams that are separate but intrinsically linked:
• Delivery vehicle: With a focus on council owned assets, and building on Glasgow's LHEES which provides a clear direction for decarbonising heat and improving building efficiency in the city, a public private partnership or concession agreement will be explored. This could see investment in areas such as low/zero-carbon heat networks, renewable energy from wind and solar, energy efficiency, and smart energy systems but can be extended to other energy related project. A critical part of the project scope will be consideration of additional social value, community involvement and ensuring a Just Transition. The full scope will be determined through competitive dialogue with the market to ascertain the most commercially viable offer for the Council.
• Climate investment vehicle: The creation of an investment vehicle for the city/city region would unlock access to capital from the private sector, as well as long-term patient capital from other sectors, such as Pension Funds. The fund would help to address the funding gap as well as providing city partners with the opportunity to progress projects that otherwise may not be able to be delivered. In addition, further mechanisms for appointing institutional investors will be assessed to allow for a more streamlined approach to mobilising investment opportunities.

In June 2023, the Scottish and UK Governments announced that the Glasgow City Region would be one of two areas to host the first Investment Zones in Scotland, supporting climate-resilient economic development and a just transition. The Glasgow City Region Investment Zone will draw on existing partnerships and a strong sense of where successful clusters of priority sectors can be amplified, benefitting from £160m of government support over the next decade through a mix of tax and spend incentives.

Key factors supporting climate-related investment and financial planning in the City of Melbourne include the adoption of an ESG Procurement Framework, which embeds environmental, social and governance principles into all purchasing decisions. This ensures climate impacts, particularly carbon emissions, are consistently considered alongside financial outcomes. The framework mandates a 10% ESG weighting in all procurement evaluations, driving investment choices that favour low-carbon suppliers and discourage links with harmful industries such as fossil fuels through positive and negative screening processes. Further, contractual requirements prioritise electric vehicle procurement and detailed reporting on transport fuel use, ensuring both direct and supply-chain emissions are addressed. These measures, together with active engagement through the Supplier Relationship Management (SRM) program, provide a structured mechanism for working closely with suppliers to achieve long-term emissions reduction. Collectively, these factors align procurement and financial planning with Council's target of net zero emissions by 2040, ensuring climate considerations are embedded in both investment and operational decisions.

Council has accessed finance from national government to support climate-related investment, such as the 2.5M received from the Federal Government's Community Energy Upgrades program, which will enable the electrification of council-owned facilities including large recreation centres, libraries, community centres, and the 150 year-old, heritage listed Melbourne Town Hall.

CoM has received funding from Bloomberg Philanthropies to deliver the Climate Action Grants program, which provides funding to young people aged 15-25 to design and deliver climate-focused projects in their communities. YCAF is underpinned by youth empowerment principles, young people are supported through capacity building, building personal and professional capital and creating a community of passionate young people.

The City of Melbourne's Urban Forest Fund enables partnerships and contributions towards new greening projects in the city, beyond Council's existing capital works program. Contributions to the Urban Forest Fund are welcomed from organisations or individuals wanting to create a greener and more liveable Melbourne into the future. CoM created the Urban Forest Fund to accelerate greening across through partnerships between government and the private sector.

We also reduce fossil fuel use by ensuring that wherever practical, and as a first principle, all new vehicle purchases or leases must be electric. We work with suppliers to improve how they report on transport fuels from subcontractors.

column17:
The City of Johannesburg holds a Ba3 rating with a stable outlook from Moody's as of April 2025. The rating reflects Johannesburg's strong financial base, underpinned by a large and diversified economy that contributes around 16% of South Africa's GDP. The city demonstrates sound debt management and continues to post operating surpluses, with an 8.3% surplus in 2024 and a projected 7.1% in 2025. Its revenue structure is robust, with 81% generated from own sources such as service charges and property taxes, while government grants make up 14%.
Despite these strengths, Johannesburg faces serious infrastructure challenges, including a water infrastructure backlog of ZAR24.2 billion and an electricity backlog of ZAR40 billion. These pressures are compounded by high unemployment, service delivery shortfalls, and climate-related risks such as drought and water shortages. Debt levels, while stable at about 25% of operating revenue, remain moderately high. Liquidity weakened to 3.5% in 2024 but is expected to recover toward 2026 as financial strategies take effect.
From an ESG perspective, Johannesburg carries a CIS-4 score, reflecting significant environmental and social risks, particularly in water management and inequality. Governance, however, is a relative strength, with the city maintaining unqualified audits and transparent financial reporting. Overall, the stable outlook signals resilience, but future rating changes will depend on consistent improvements in liquidity and operating performance, as well as broader sovereign rating movements.

The HKMA actively supports responsible investment through incorporation of ESG factors, with particular emphasis on climate change and net-zero transition, into its investment processes for the Exchange Fund. Underpinned by the guiding principle that prioritises ESG investments when long-term risk-adjusted returns are comparable, the HKMA has invested in a wide variety of green and sustainable investments across public and private markets. The HKMA has a target of net-zero emissions by 2050 for the Investment Portfolio of the Exchange Fund. In October 2024, the HKMA published the Sustainable Finance Action Agenda to reinforce its commitment to net-zero emissions and support climate transition in Asia. Notably, the HKMA will endeavour to reduce the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund's public equity holdings by 67% by 2030 from the 2017 level. As at end-2023, the WACI of its public equity holdings has achieved a 50% reduction compared to 2017, outperforming the market investment benchmark. In addition, to enhance transparency for its counterparties and service providers, including for example, issuers or counterparties of financial instruments, external managers and general partners, regarding management of sustainability-related matters, the HKMA launched the inaugural HKMA ESG Expectations in 2024, outlining the preferred practices structuring around five key pillars: governance and resources, ESG framework and policy, engagement, voting, as well as disclosure and reporting.

Os programas do PPA relacionados às mudanças climáticas são o 3005 - Promoção da Sustentabilidade Ambiental, 3008 - Gestão dos Riscos e Promoção da Resiliência a Desastres e Eventos Críticos, 3009 - Melhoria da Mobilidade Urbana Universal, 3015 - Promoção da Cidade como Referência Global e Destino Turístico, 3019 - Promoção do Crescimento Econômico e Geração de Postos de Trabalho e Oportunidades, 3022 - Requalificação e Promoção da Ocupação dos Espaços Públicos. As dotações orçamentárias desses programas viabilizaram a realização de ações do PPA que contribuem diretamente para a consecução das estratégias do PlanClima SP, direcionando recursos fiscais do município para a mitigação e adaptação às mudanças climáticas.\n\nO município conta também com recursos do Fundo Especial de Meio Ambiente e Desenvolvimento Sustentável (FEMA), vinculado à Secretaria do Verde e Meio Ambiente (SVMA), que destina-se a apoiar projetos de uso sustentável de recursos naturais, manutenção, recuperação e melhoria da qualidade ambiental. Tais recursos podem ser partilhados por órgãos públicos e organizações da sociedade civil cujos projetos tenham sido aprovados pelo Conselho do Fundo Especial do Meio Ambiente e Desenvolvimento Sustentável (Confema). Seus recursos são provenientes de dotações orçamentárias específicas, multas por infrações ambientais, doações de pessoas físicas ou jurídicas, doações de entidades internacionais, entre outras fontes. Em 2023, a execução orçamentária liquidada do Fundo foi de R$ 51,7 milhões, em atividades como construção e implantação de parques urbanos e lineares, construção e implantação de Unidades de Conservação, entre outras.

Em 2024, a Prefeitura do Município de São Paulo realizou diversas ações para descarbonizar os investimentos municipais, incentivando também as concessionárias de serviços públicos a reduzirem suas emissões de gases de efeito estufa (GEE). Uma das estratégias setoriais prioritárias foi a redução das emissões de poluentes e GEE pela frota de ônibus do transporte público municipal. Duas iniciativas da Meta 68 do Programa de Metas 2021-2024 - reduzir em 40% a emissão de material particulado e em 12% a emissão de dióxido de carbono pelo sistema de transporte público municipal - foram atingidas e a redução em 25% da emissão de óxidos de nitrogênio encontra-se em execução. Apenas em 2023, R$ 103,70 milhões foram utilizados na aquisição de ônibus municipais movidos por energia limpa. Investimentos de R$ 2,11 milhões em 2022 e R$ 5,84 milhões em 2023 estruturaram 464 hortas urbanas baseadas em tecnologias ambientais, com capacitações ligadas à economia verde, atendendo a Meta 61 do Programa de Metas 2021-2024.

Além disso, segundo o Relatório de Acompanhamento do PPA 2022-2025 referente ao exercício financeiro de 2023, foram destinados R$ 2,6 milhões em ações de fiscalização, monitoramento e controle ambiental, R$ 900 mil em educação ambiental, R$ 4,2 milhões na implantação e construção de Ecopontos, R$ 21,1 milhões na construção de ciclovias, ciclofaixas e ciclorrotas, R$ 27 milhões na construção de implantação de Parques Urbanos e Lineares, entre outros investimentos de descarbonização.

O município vem também tomando iniciativas normativas e regulatórias para incentivar que os investimentos do setor privado na cidade contribuam para a descarbonização da economia. Entre as metas do PlanClima SP está incluir ações relacionadas à mitigação das mudanças climáticas nas exigências do licenciamento ambiental e do estudo de impacto de vizinhança de empreendimentos e o estabelecimento de critérios que orientem a destinação de recursos dos fundos municipais para ações de mitigação.

2. 전담 조직·거버넌스
1)창원시 탄소중립지원센터 운영 → 재정 집행 관리, 사업 발굴·조정 허브
2)시민·산업·공공 협력형 구조 → 민관 협력사업의 재정 분담 기반 마련
3)국제 네트워크 참여(CDP, GCoM) → 글로벌 펀드·사업 연계 가능성 확대

3. 재정 확보 수단
1)지방비 편성: 기후·환경국 및 관련 부서별 연차예산 반영
2)국비 공모사업: 환경부·산업부·농식품부 등 국책 재정사업(도시숲, 수소충전소, 순환경제, 에너지 전환 등) 확보
3)탄소중립 기금 및 특별회계: 정부 차원의 기후대응기금 연계, 향후 활용 가능성
4)녹색금융 연계: KDB산업은행, IBK 등 금융기관 ESG 대출·투자 활용

4. 민간 및 지역사회 참여
1)기업 탄소저감 컨설팅 및 현장 보조금 지원(중소기업 전환 지원)

3)재생에너지 보급 확대 → 민간발전사, 에너지협동조합 투자 유치

1)온실가스 인벤토리 및 배출 통계 구축 → 투자 효과 분석 기반

column17: In 2015, the Environmental Protection Administration of Taiwan established the \'Greenhouse Gas Offset Project Management Regulations\' to encourage the reduction of emissions, and to grant reduction credits (carbon rights) after verification and review by a third party. With reference to the United Nations Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), a new category of \'micro-scale offset projects\' was added in 2018 to encourage small and medium-sized enterprises and other small emission sources, and to expand the participation of the transportation and residential and commercial sectors to promote the development of emission reduction technologies for all types of sources.Taipei City and Taipei 101 are working together to reduce carbon emissions, and this is the first example of micro-scale offset for the residential and commercial sector in Taiwan. The City assisted Taipei 101 in replacing the lighting in the underground parking lot of the commercial office building in 2020, and upgrading 2,841 T5 fluorescent lighting fixtures to high-efficiency LED lighting fixtures. It is estimated that the reduction of electricity consumption by 510,000 kWh per year will result in a total of 2,718 tons of carbon reduction in 10 years, and each side will receive 50% of the carbon rights, and 92 tons of carbon rights were obtained in 2021. In 2021, the City actively assisted the Carrefour Chongqing Store in taking stock of the efficiency of its air-conditioning equipment, and proposed a project to replace its high-efficiency magnetic floating ice and water machine, saving an average of 343,000 kWh of electricity per year. It is the first case in the country where a large retailer completed a micro-scale offset.The City will continue to work with businesses to promote the micro-scale offset program, leading more large corporate customers to follow through and move toward a net zero future.

As previously noted, the City continues to support the divestment of financial assets from fossil fuels and investing in climate-friendly opportunities through the implementation of the City's Cash Management and Investment Policy which prohibits investments “in instruments which consist of assets and activities whose value is realised through the release of unmitigated high levels of carbon dioxide”. In support of this, external fund managers appointed by the City are required to sign an annual compliance certificate that confirms adherence to all the elements of the City's investment criteria as outlined by the Cash Management and Investment Policy. Furthermore, through its Climate Change Strategy (2021), the City has committed to “use financial mechanisms, including business models, tariffs, investment and divestment to respond to climate change impacts and mitigation opportunities” (Goal 31). This is further detailed in the City's Climate Change Action Plan, which states that the City will “support the call for responsible divestment by taking steps where possible to divest financial assets from fossil fuels, or reinvest in climate-friendly activities.”

At the end of July 2024, the City's investments amounted to R15 986 601 000 spread between the external Investment Managers and compliant with the divestment clause of the City's Cash Management and Investment Policy. 

With the help of C40, the City convened a session in 2023/24 with the city pension funds of London and New York to engage with two of the larger affiliated pension funds of City of Cape Town employees on the divest/invest approaches taken. The exchange demonstrated that affiliated pension funds are considerably far along the environmental, social and governance (ESG) journey, and that they are interested in continuous sharing of information around investments with poor ESG (specifically carbon) records to help reduce holdings in these investments.

In addition to our cash investments, the City has developed a ten year, ZAR 140 billion (US$ 7.5 billion) infrastructure pipeline informed by sector plans. These sector plans are responsive to developmental needs as well as to impacts of the climate crisis, for example, the water sector plan includes measures to increase the availability and supply of water to allow for a 1 in 100 year drought scenario.

column15: The City of Miami employs a diversified and strategic financing approach to support climate-related planning and infrastructure investments, combining local funding with state, federal, and private-sector sources. Central to this strategy is the $400 million Miami Forever Bond, of which approximately $192 million is dedicated to flood mitigation, stormwater upgrades, and shoreline protection, particularly in vulnerable neighborhoods. The City actively secures grants from programs such as FDEP's Resilient Florida, FEMA's BRIC and HMGP, NFWF's National Coastal Resilience Fund, and CDBG-MIT to co-finance large-scale resilience projects. Public-private partnerships (P3) further extend the City's capacity, with key collaborations involving FPL for electric vehicle infrastructure and solar initiatives, developers incentivized through resilience-focused zoning, and research institutions supporting climate modeling and pilot programs. Through its Capital Improvements Program, Miami mandates that all infrastructure projects incorporate sea-level rise projections, storm surge modeling, and resilience guidelines. Additionally, the City is exploring green bonds, stormwater utility fee reforms, and TIFs to create sustainable funding streams for long-term adaptation, ensuring investments are aligned with climate risk reduction and equitable outcomes.

column17: The City of Miami maintains strong credit ratings from major U.S. credit rating agencies, reflecting sound fiscal management and the City's ability to meet its financial obligations. As of 2024, the City holds an AA rating from S&P Global Ratings and an Aa2 rating from Moody's Investors Service, both of which indicate high credit quality and low credit risk. While Fitch Ratings previously rated the City, that rating was formally withdrawn in 2023 following an internal restructuring of the City's debt portfolio and a consolidation of its rating agency relationships. In recent years, credit rating agencies have increasingly incorporated climate risk and resilience planning into their assessments of municipal creditworthiness. The City of Miami has proactively responded to information requests from S&P and Moody's regarding its climate adaptation strategies, sea-level rise projections, and capital investments related to flood mitigation, emergency preparedness, and infrastructure resilience. These efforts have helped position Miami as a forward-looking municipality that is taking concrete action to reduce long-term climate exposure. Agencies have recognized the City's voter-approved Miami Forever Bond ($400 million) in 2018, with nearly half allocated to sea-level rise and flood prevention measures, as a positive indicator of local political support and institutional commitment to resilience. Additionally, the City's ongoing engagement with federal and state climate funding sources, such as the Resilient Florida Program and FEMA's BRIC grants, has further reinforced the City's risk-mitigation profile and fiscal capacity to address future environmental hazards. Overall, the City's strong credit ratings enhance its ability to issue general obligation bonds at favorable interest rates, reduce the cost of borrowing for critical climate infrastructure, and sustain long-term financial planning aligned with resilience and equity goals.

column19: In 2021, the City of Miami began exploring the divestment of fossil fuel holdings from its pension fund portfolios, aligning with broader climate action goals and the growing movement toward sustainable investment practices. The initiative received early support from elected officials who advocated for responsible environmental stewardship and sought to reduce the City's financial exposure to carbon-intensive industries. As part of this effort, City staff and advisors initiated a review of existing investment allocations, evaluated alternative ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance)-focused investment vehicles, and consulted with fund managers to assess fiduciary implications. However, due to the complexity of pension governance structures, market conditions, and competing financial priorities, the divestment strategy was paused, with the City maintaining an interest in revisiting the issue in the future as market opportunities and legislative frameworks evolve to better support fossil-free municipal investment policies.

column19: The Phoenix employee retirement fund must invest in the most profitable investments regardless of carbon intensity; Phoenix does not have the authority to mandate divestment of fossil fuels from the employees' retirement fund. However, the investment policy of the City of Phoenix is intended to provide for the prudent and efficient investment of the City's temporarily idle cash while safely maximizing returns within carefully defined investment parameters. The investment policies and practices of the City are based on guidelines mandated by Arizona State statute, the Phoenix City Code, and prudent money management. For City funds, the City's investment objectives, in order of priority, are 1) safety, 2) liquidity, and 3) yield, with the objective of attaining a competitive rate of return given the constraints of safety and liquidity. As such, the $5 billion portfolio of City funds is primarily in US Treasuries, US Government Agency Securities, and repurchase agreements backed by collateral in US Treasuries. The City also holds funds in other permitted investments, including municipal obligations, US Government or municipal money market funds, certificates of deposits, and mortgage-backed securities (MBS) issued or guaranteed by a US government agency. Included in the MBS, the City currently holds $30 million in bonds issued by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac that have been designated “green”. Due to the nature of fixed income investments required by the City's investment policy, the City holds no investments in fossil fuels.

Salvador tem utilizado diferentes mecanismos para acessar financiamentos relacionados ao clima, visando viabilizar ações de mitigação, adaptação e resiliência climática no território municipal. Esses mecanismos envolvem desde a elaboração de projetos estruturados com critérios de sustentabilidade até a integração da política climática com o planejamento orçamentário da cidade.
Um dos principais caminhos adotados é a estruturação de projetos que atendem aos critérios exigidos por financiadores nacionais e internacionais, como o Banco Mundial, o Banco Interamericano de Desenvolvimento (BID), a GIZ (Agência Alemã de Cooperação Técnica) e o Banco de Desenvolvimento da América Latina (CAF). Esses projetos estão ligados a áreas como mobilidade urbana sustentável, infraestrutura resiliente, requalificação de áreas de risco e soluções baseadas na natureza.
Além disso, a cidade participa ativamente de redes e programas internacionais que apoiam governos locais no enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas, como o Pacto Global de Prefeitos pelo Clima e a Energia (GCoM), o ICLEI (Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade) e o CDP (Carbon Disclosure Project), o que não apenas fortalece a visibilidade da cidade, como também a torna elegível para editais e fundos climáticos voltados a cidades comprometidas com metas de descarbonização e resiliência.
Salvador tem apostado na cooperação técnica internacional como estratégia preparatória para o acesso a financiamentos. Parcerias com instituições como a GIZ, o World Resources Institute (WRI) e o C40 Cities Finance Facility têm contribuído para a qualificação técnica de projetos e fortalecimento institucional da cidade. O uso de ferramentas como inventários de emissões de gases de efeito estufa, mapas de vulnerabilidade climática e indicadores ambientais também fornece uma base técnica robusta que confere credibilidade aos projetos apresentados e aumenta a chance de captação de recursos.

A cidade de Salvador possui uma classificação de crédito considerada excelente, com destaque em avaliações nacionais que atestam sua capacidade de pagamento e responsabilidade fiscal. Essas classificações são fundamentais para o acesso a financiamentos públicos e internacionais, especialmente em áreas estratégicas como infraestrutura urbana e ação climática.

O principal indicador utilizado pelo Governo Federal para avaliar a capacidade de crédito dos entes subnacionais é o Índice de Capacidade de Pagamento (CAPAG), elaborado pela Secretaria do Tesouro Nacional. Em maio de 2024, Salvador conquistou pela primeira vez a nota máxima “A+” no CAPAG, resultado que reflete o bom desempenho da gestão fiscal em três dimensões: endividamento, liquidez e poupança corrente. Essa classificação garante à cidade a possibilidade de contratar operações de crédito com garantia da União, o que amplia significativamente seu acesso a recursos de instituições financeiras nacionais e internacionais.

Além disso, Salvador também obteve destaque no Índice Firjan de Gestão Fiscal (IFGF), publicado em 2023, liderando entre as capitais brasileiras. A cidade alcançou uma nota geral de 0,9823, em uma escala que vai de 0 a 1, com desempenho máximo nos indicadores de autonomia, gastos com pessoal, liquidez e investimentos. O IFGF avalia a eficiência da gestão fiscal com base em dados oficiais disponibilizados pelas próprias prefeituras ao Tesouro Nacional, e a posição de Salvador nesse ranking evidencia a capacidade da cidade de gerar receitas próprias, investir e manter equilíbrio nas contas públicas.

City of Ottawa Green Bonds

City of Ottawa green debentures are used to finance capital works that promote environmentally sustainable development across the City to mitigate or adapt to the effects of climate change and/or contribute to the reduction of greenhouse gases. The net proceeds of a Green Debenture issuance will be used to fund capital projects identified as eligible projects under the City of Ottawa Green Debenture Framework. 

Without limitation, capital projects in the following sectors will generally be considered eligible:
- renewable energy
- infrastructure energy efficiency
- pollution prevention and control
- clean transportation
- sustainable water management
- sustainable management of natural resources
- climate change adaptation and resilience
- green buildings

https://ottawa.ca/en/business/research-and-data/investor-relations/green-bonds-city-ottawa

City of Ottawa Municipal Budget Climate Lens

The City applies a climate lens to the annual financial budget to qualitatively assess which capital investments will contribute to reduce GHG emissions or build climate resiliency. The 2024 Budget was the second consecutive budget cycle that a climate lens was applied to all new capital budget requests. This systematic approach identified how new investments contribute to climate goals and where future opportunities might exist. Overall, 155 capital budget requests were rated as having a climate contribution in the 2024 Draft Budget. Of these, 24 were identified as going beyond business-as-planned or business-as-usual and were rated as having a moderate or major contribution, totalling more than $278 million of new investments. This is an increase of $226 million from Budget 2023.

City of Ottawa Climate Related Financial Disclosures

The City of Ottawa voluntarily discloses its climate-related actions, strategies, and financial impacts as part of its annual finance reports to help stakeholders and decision-makers understand how the City is responding to climate-related risks and opportunities. The disclosures also explain how the City incorporates climate-related information into the strategic, capital, and financial planning processes. The last disclosure was included in the 2023 Annual Report

Therefore, the Municipality conducted consultations with municipal entities and Porto Climate Pact subscribers, aligning investments with city decarbonization goals. Traditional reliance on subsidies and public funding may not be sustainable or enough to meet the ambitious climate goals. Seeking alternative sources of financing becomes imperative to diversify funding streams. The city is exploring the need for innovative financing mechanisms that go beyond conventional approaches. This could involve the development of new financial instruments, partnerships, or models that can mobilize funds without solely relying on public subsidies, such as: -Green Finance Incentives: Implementing incentives for financial institutions and investors to prioritize green and sustainable investments. -Green Bonds: Encouraging the issuance of climate bonds to fund specific projects related to renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable infrastructure, and other climate-friendly initiatives. -Green Innovation Funds: Establishing funds specifically dedicated to financing innovative climate solutions. -Eco-friendly Real Estate Development: Encouraging sustainable and energy-efficient building practices through regulatory frameworks and incentives. The development of the Environmental Index of Porto is currently underway, aiming to incentivize project developers in recovery, rehabilitation, and construction to incorporate natural solutions into their projects. Two scenarios were simulated using the Sustainable Asset Valuation (SAVi) assessment model with a timeline from 2024 to 2050: Nature-based Infrastructure (NBI) scenario 1 which integrates the new blue carbon strategy with mangrove restoration and is based on elements of the SAVi assessment that are detailed in the previous sections, such as the climate data analysis and the spatial analysis, and NBI scenario 2 which is based on the more ambitious target of planting 5 million trees by 2030. Based on the SAVi analysis, the #TreeTown NBI project is economically viable, generating discounted net benefits of USD 21.68 million in NBI scenario 1 and USD 26.45 million in NBI scenario 2 by 2050. For each dollar invested, the interventions generate USD 2.14 and USD 2.04 in economic, social, and environmental benefits for the two NBI scenarios respectively. The avoided infrastructure damages from floods, landslides, coastal erosion, and sea-level rise (undiscounted values are USD 30.25 million for NBI scenario 1 and USD 39.27 million for NBI scenario 2) alone make up for the construction and maintenance costs (USD 22.10 million in NBI scenario 1 and USD 30.00 million in NBI scenario), underlining the economic viability and climate adaptation benefits. Avoided infrastructure damages from coastal erosion are responsible for 48% of the total avoided infrastructure damages, followed by avoided damages from flooding (31%), sea level rise (17%) and landslides, which were only responsible for 4% of total avoided infrastructure damages. Planting and maintaining the trees creates jobs and about USD 8.23 million in income in NBI scenario 1 and USD 10.76 million in NBI scenario 2, increasing prosperity in the community. Income creation from employment, or discretionary spending, represents the amount of money that flows back into the economy in the form of additional consumption. Planting and O&M of the trees leads to employment creation, which has beneficial socio-economic impacts, such as increased discretionary spending. To address credit worthiness and to attract investment in the Freetown Natural Capital Investment Strategy, Freetown is working with partners through Bloomberg Philanthropies to value its natural capital and create financing, operating and funding model to be implemented through a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) and a TreeTown Fund that operates independent of city operations and therefore not tied to the city's credit rating. The capital structure of the #FreeTownTheTreeTown fund is designed to be adaptive and inclusive, utilizing a mix of equity and debt instruments tailored to the needs of the projects. At a project level the capital stack will enable assets to be subdivided while at portfolio level recombined to be optimally balanced for investor returns. 
•	A Units (Dynamic Equity): These units are flexible, adjusting based on the contribution and involvement of the holders in proportion to the labor and capital investment. They are ideal for participants who play an active role in governance or operations, with their value reflecting the performance and contributions only once the project is de-risked and certain performance-based milestones are achieved. 
•	C Units (Fixed Equity): Representing stable ownership with rights to capital appreciation, these units can be linked to TreeTown Impact Tokens, allowing token holders to convert them into C Units, thus fostering long-term investment in ecological projects.
•	D Units (Convertible Debt): These units offer downside protection with the potential to convert into equity upon reaching certain financial milestones. They are particularly suited for early-stage investments where the investor seeks both security and the possibility of future equity participation but who don't have the tolerance to invest pre valuation.
•	P Units (Profit Units): Designed to provide a share of profits without directly granting ownership rights, P Units are useful for incentivizing non-member contributors or contractors. They align compensation with the project's profitability, encouraging performance-based engagement. Each of these units must be structured to comply with relevant securities laws and regulations, ensuring legal and regulatory alignment while enabling flexibility in the fund's operations and the flexibility of a capital system with the functionality of these asset classes can enable a seamless integration between the fund's governance and TreeTown Impact Tokens in the contexts of the emergent carbon market.

As outlined in the Mayor's programme 2021-2025, Turku has taken climate budgeting into use. By sustainable investment principles and practices, the carbon footprint of investments will be reduced. During the 2025-2030 economic plan period, the total amount of investments supporting climate goals will be approximately EUR 1.7 billion. EU taxonomy is used as a evaluation framework for climate related investments because city of Turku is seeking a significant part of its funding from the European Investment Bank.

City of Turku is currently running several projects developing climate budgeting further as a tool for preparing, steering and monitoring the City Group's investment programme, combining climate goals and the implementation of the circular economy.

According to Turku Climate Plan 2029:-Investment projects of the Turku City Group will be examined comprehensively in normal planning and decision-making processes, looking at the entire life cycle. Not only costs but also climate impacts will be taken into consideration.
-Where possible, the EU taxonomy will be taken into consideration when making investments, so that green funding can also be utilised.
-In investments and procurement, the City of Turku will seek to promote circular economy solutions and reduce consumption of natural resources.
-Sufficient resources will be allocated and sufficient expertise ensured for examining the climate impacts of investments and for implementing responsible investments.
-The visibility of climate-responsible investments in communications and in the national media will be enhanced.

Muito antes do Brasil discutir os impactos das mudanças climáticas nas gestões públicas, o Programa Lagoas do Norte já efetivava o investimento em adaptação. Ele foi a primeira grande experiência que a cidade de Teresina realizou com intervenções multissetoriais integradas.
Com financiamento do Banco Mundial, a Prefeitura de Teresina fez os estudos sobre os impactos das águas dos rios Parnaíba e Poti e das lagoas que banham a zona norte. As águas, que antes causavam enchentes e alagamentos, foram disciplinadas através de canais, desobstrução das margens das lagoas, instalação de comportas e diversas ações junto à população.

A elaboração do Plano de Ação Climática também foi realizada através de financiamento. O trabalho foi desenvolvido pela Agenda Teresina 2030, vinculada à Semplan, com financiamento do CAF - Banco de Desenvolvimento da América Latina.

Teresina se envolveu com redes globais de cidades, como o Pacto Global de Prefeitos pelo Clima e Energia e o ICLEI- Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade, CAF, Agência Francesa de
Desenvolvimento (AFD), ONU-Habitat e outros.

column15: Hamilton's Climate Action Strategy is Hamilton's most ambitious climate plan to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and become a national leader in climate adaptation. It is comprised of two important plans including: “ReCharge Hamilton - Our Community Energy and Emissions Plan” (CEEP). This included a community-wide analysis of energy and emissions based on 2016. Through understanding existing energy and emissions the City worked with leading consultants SSG through their CityInSight Model to develop a Low-Carbon Scenario including a list of actions to achieve net-zero GHG emissions by 2050; and “Hamilton's Climate Change Impact Adaptation Plan” (CCIAP). This included working with ICLEI Canada through the Building Adaptable Resilient Communities (BARC) 5-milestone framework. This included understanding the future climate scenarios using global and regional climate scenarios using many future emissions scenarios downscaled to the local level. Through this analysis climate risk statements were created and an community-wide Vulnerability and Risk Assessment (VRA) was completed and identified the top risks for Hamilton. These risks were then used to inform the objective and actions within the CCIAP.In order to proceed with implementation and completion of Hamilton's Climate Action Strategy and the complex actions within it, we will need sources of funding from all levels of government, including private equity.

S&P's report highlights Kingston's diversified economy and robust population growth, along with strong political continuity and consensus in developing strategic priorities and passing budgets. The report also identifies the City's strong corporate financial management practices, the use of four-year operating budgets and 15-year capital plans, as well as an experienced and qualified management team in place to enact financial policies. 

The AA+ (stable outlook) rating is the second-highest bond rating assigned by the agency.

2、2022年8月南沙成功获批国家级气候投融资试点资格以来，广州南沙大胆创新，先行探索以气候金融牵引企业低碳转型、赋能实体经济高质量发展，打造以国际气候金融中心为特色的气候投融资“南沙模式”。该模式连续两年获评广东自贸试验区最佳制度创新案例，获评2024年度广东绿色金融改革创新推广案例。一是有力推动了粤港澳大湾区气候投融资标准融合规则衔接。出台国内首套穗港澳合作的气候投融资领域标准《企业（项目）融资气候友好评价规范》，成立粤港澳大湾区应对气候变化标准联盟，汇聚南方电网、广东省能源集团等10余家能源、电力、石化、汽车制造等行业代表性企业，共同推进应对气候变化领域标准国际化。国家碳计量中心（广东）成功落户南沙，辐射带动粤港澳三地碳市场数据、标准、认证等方面协同互认。

To achieve Quezon City's GHG emissions reduction goal under the ambitious scenario of 30 percent by 2030 (relative to the BAU scenario), the carbon budget must be slashed by 3.6 million MtCO2e (Quezon City, 2021). A critical pathway to achieving this is through the mobilization of green financing towards carbon-smart policies and other low carbon investments in the private sector.

The Quezon City Climate Investment Opportunities Diagnostic Report consider four (4) measures the City can encourage private participation in the city's sustainable development via the mobilization of local, private financial resources:
1. Improve Building Code - Mandate a Green Building Code that covers 95 percent of new, private non-residential buildings, specifying a 10 percent energy savings relative to BAU along with water-efficient fixtures.
2. Incentivize Green Building Certification and Energy Efficiency in New Buildings - Encourage private developers and owner-operators to obtain Green Building Certification, such as IFC's EDGE, for 70 percent of new, private residential buildings, saving 20 percent of energy use relative to BAU.
3. Leverage Finance for Private EVs - Facilitate lending through local FIs to cover the cost of capital for 20,000 privately-owned EVs, expected to be the equivalent of 16 percent of all private vehicles in Quezon City in 2030.
4. Mobilize Financing for Private Rooftop Rainwater Harvesting - Facilitate lending through local FIs to cover the cost of rooftop rainwater harvesting on 22 percent of the city's private rooftops.

In total, these measures will cost USD 803 million. The aforementioned low-carbon investments would be mobilized through Green Financing by developers, industries, local businesses, and private consumers, and may be enabled with Lending through Local Financial Intermediaries.

The City of Tampere primarily invests through investment funds, delegating individual company-level investment decisions to fund managers. The City requires all fund managers to adhere to the UN Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI). In accordance with these principles, fund managers are expected to integrate Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors into their investment processes and to promote ESG reporting among investee companies.

Each fund manager applies their own sustainability screening criteria — such as exclusion lists, restricted sectors, or limits on exposure to fossil fuel companies. To ensure compliance, the City of Tampere requires fund managers to provide an annual sustainability report for each investment fund.

When selecting new investment funds, the City emphasizes alignment with its strategic goals, particularly its carbon neutrality target. Preference is given to funds that explicitly exclude companies involved in fossil fuel production if their operations are not aligned with the City's climate objectives.

In addition to fund-level sustainability, the City encourages fund managers to demonstrate corporate responsibility by publishing an annual corporate sustainability report. Other key mechanisms for monitoring responsibility include active engagement with fund managers and ongoing monitoring through various communication channels.

The City of Tampere also participates in collaborative initiatives with other institutional investors to promote responsible investment. By attending seminars and forums, the City seeks to network with other actors committed to advancing sustainable investment practices.

Sunderland City Council does not have its own individual pension fund, instead the council and its employees participate within the Tyne and Wear Pension Fund. The Council has a single representative (18 representatives in total) on the Tyne and Wear Pension Fund Committee. The Pension Committee has undertaken action on behalf of the Tyne and Wear Pension Fund and commits to transitioning its investment portfolios to net-zero GHG emissions by 2050 or sooner and to reduce emissions by 50% - 60% by 2030 based upon the 2019 baseline calculated in the carbon footprint analysis.
In addition, a reduction of 30% - 35% will be targeted by 2025 and reporting against these targets will be published annually.
The Fund also commits to undertake climate based financial risk assessments and to report the results as part of an annual Task Force for Climate Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) Report.
In order to ensure that the Fund achieves its targets it will undertake an annual carbon footprint analysis and regularly report on the progress being made.
In addition, the Fund will undertake a triennial review of the medium and long term targets to ensure that they remain appropriate and challenging, given the ever changing, economic, environmental and technological environment. 
The review will look for opportunities to bring forward the Net Zero targets where this is considered reasonable.
The Fund also commits to working with other investors along with its investment managers to promote the change necessary and to pursue efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C set out in the Paris Agreement. This includes the 
The Pension Fund also commits to achieving net-zero GHG emissions on its own operations by 2030.

The carbon footprint analysis work undertaken by the Fund shows that the Fund continues to make excellent progress in reducing Weighted Average Carbon Intensity (WACI) with a 39% reduction over the four year period, from 2019 to 2023. This is the Fund's primary risk metric. This represents an improvement of 18% from 2023. The Fund has now achieved its first interim carbon emissions reduction target of a 30-35% reduction by 2025, two years ahead of schedule. 

Further information on the Tyne and Wear Pension Fund's approach to climate change can be found at: Climate change - Tyne and Wear Pension Fund (twpf.info) and https://www.twpf.info/article/10105/Climate-change-policy

Na jurisdição de Braga, vários fatores apoiam o investimento e o planejamento financeiro relacionados às alterações climáticas, promovendo a resiliência e a sustentabilidade dos projetos.
Braga tem acesso a fundos nacionais e regionais destinados a iniciativas de adaptação e mitigação das alterações climáticas. O Programa Operacional de Sustentabilidade e Eficiência no Uso de Recursos (POSEUR) é um exemplo significativo, apoiando projetos de infraestrutura verde e eficiência hídrica.

As parcerias entre o setor público e privado são fundamentais para mobilizar recursos financeiros e expertise técnica, permitindo a implementação de projetos ambiciosos que, de outra forma, seriam inviáveis. Incentivos fiscais ajudam a atrair investimentos privados.

A cidade beneficia de diversas iniciativas da União Europeia, como o Fundo Europeu Agrícola para o Desenvolvimento Rural (FEADER) e o Horizonte Europa, que oferecem recursos financeiros significativos para projetos de adaptação e mitigação.

O uso de plataformas de crowdfunding tem crescido, permitindo que a comunidade local financie projetos climáticos, engajando cidadãos e empresas em iniciativas sustentáveis.

O município implementa incentivos fiscais para promover investimentos em tecnologias verdes, estimulando empresas e indivíduos a adotarem soluções que reduzam a pegada de carbono.

Braga colabora com instituições financeiras para criar linhas de crédito específicas para projetos sustentáveis, facilitando o acesso a financiamentos.

Esses mecanismos e estratégias são essenciais para promover um desenvolvimento sustentável e resiliente em Braga, garantindo que os projetos relacionados com o clima sejam viáveis e eficazes.

1. Self-funded or budgeted, and establishment of a climate fund — Green Budget and Climate Fund of New Taipei City
New Taipei City will allocate at least NT$20 billion annually as part of its green budget to drive private green investments and green job opportunities. Additionally, a “New Taipei Climate Fund” will be established, with its main sources of income being the carbon fees collected by the Environmental Protection Administration and voluntary donations from enterprises. The fund will be open to applications from communities, enterprises, households, and schools to support energy efficiency improvements, renewable energy installations, and energy transition projects. The City will also apply for international carbon credit certification for the emission reductions achieved through its policy measures to assist both the municipal government and enterprises in achieving carbon neutrality.

In response to global net-zero and carbon tariff trends, Taiwan's central government announced in 2021 that achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 is a national development goal. El financiamiento para inversiones relacionadas con el cambio climático en la comuna de Punta Arenas enfrenta un escenario complejo, marcado por la necesidad de articular recursos limitados con múltiples prioridades municipales. La acción climática requiere inversiones en infraestructura verde, eficiencia energética, movilidad sostenible, gestión de residuos y protección de ecosistemas, todas medidas contempladas en el PACCC, lo que implica planificación financiera estratégica y sostenida.

Actualmente, la comuna ha dado pasos importantes, como la creación de una glosa presupuestaria específica para acción climática, lo que permite financiar proyectos de educación ambiental, eficiencia energética y adaptación, y sienta las bases para su fortalecimiento en años futuros. Sin embargo, la dependencia de recursos externos, como fondos sectoriales del gobierno central, programas regionales y cooperación público-privada, genera incertidumbre sobre la continuidad y escala de las inversiones, especialmente frente a las demandas crecientes de la comunidad y la complejidad de los proyectos.

Este contexto exige que la planificación financiera municipal integre criterios de sostenibilidad y priorización de proyectos climáticos, asegurando que los recursos disponibles se utilicen de manera eficiente y que los proyectos más estratégicos, con mayor impacto en mitigación y adaptación, puedan ejecutarse de forma efectiva. Asimismo, es fundamental explorar mecanismos innovadores de financiamiento y alianzas multisectoriales para superar las limitaciones presupuestarias y garantizar la implementación de la acción climática a largo plazo.

Catbalogan City presently employs a blended approach in financing climate-related projects, recognizing both the potential and limitations of its fiscal capacity. The city allocates resources from its own funds, primarily the General Fund, the 20% Development Fund, and the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund, to ensure the continuity of core climate resilience initiatives such as disaster preparedness, coastal resource management, and green infrastructure. However, given the constraints of a modest local revenue base and competing service delivery priorities, these allocations are often insufficient to finance large-scale or transformative climate actions.

To bridge this gap, Catbalogan leverages national government support. Access to earmarked grants and special financing windows from agencies such as DENR, DILG, and DPWH enables the city to pursue projects that would otherwise be beyond its means, such as reforestation programs, solid waste management facilities, and resilient infrastructure development. Borrowing from the national government remains an available instrument, but it is pursued cautiously due to repayment risks and the city's prioritization of fiscal stability.

Overall, this layered financing strategy underscores Catbalogan's approach of using local funds for continuity and ownership, while maximizing national grants and technical assistance for scale and innovation. By doing so, the city enhances its adaptive capacity and ensures that climate-related investments remain aligned with both local development priorities and national policy frameworks.

Instead, priority is given to initiatives that deliver co-benefits, such as renewable energy integration in public facilities, energy-efficient retrofits of government-owned buildings, and investments in sustainable transport and waste management systems. Furthermore, Catbalogan increasingly screens development projects for their environmental and social impacts, guided by both the CLUP and the Local Climate Change Action Plan. Though a comprehensive “green investment framework” is not yet institutionalized, incremental steps such as integrating climate criteria into budgetary allocations and exploring partnerships for renewable and energy-efficient technologies, demonstrate the city's intent to decarbonize its investments over time.

Os mecanismos utilizados pela jurisdição para acessar financiamentos para projetos relacionados ao clima incluem a adesão a programas, redes e iniciativas estratégicas que ampliam o acesso a linhas de fomento nacionais e internacionais. 
O Município de Francisco Morato aderiu à Agenda 2030 da ONU e constituiu uma Comissão Interna dos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS), instrumento que organiza e integra ações locais às metas globais. Além disso, o Município é associado ao ICLEI - Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade, o que possibilita o intercâmbio técnico, a capacitação e a conexão com editais de financiamento climático. Participa, ainda, dos projetos da Rede para Desenvolvimento Urbano Sustentável (ReDUS), iniciativa que promove cooperação técnica e acesso a recursos voltados à sustentabilidade urbana. 
No âmbito nacional, Francisco Morato integra o Eixo Cidades Sustentáveis e Resilientes do Novo PAC do Governo Federal, que prevê investimentos em infraestrutura verde, resiliência climática e inclusão social. 
O município de Francisco Morato reafirma seu compromisso com as ações
climáticas por meio da adesão ao Pacto Global de Prefeitas e Prefeitos pelo Clima e
a Energia (GCoM), uma aliança internacional financiada pela União Europeia que
mobiliza cidades e governos locais no enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas, na
redução de seus impactos inevitáveis e na promoção do acesso universal à energia
segura, limpa e acessível.
Complementarmente, o município busca estabelecer parcerias e incentivos junto a fundos internacionais de interesse climático, ampliando suas possibilidades de captação de recursos e atração de investimentos voltados à transição sustentável. Essas iniciativas, somadas a outras parcerias estratégicas, fortalecem a capacidade institucional do município de captar recursos e estruturar projetos que enfrentem os desafios das mudanças climáticas.

column15: All significant financial decisions made by the WMCA must be approved by the WMCA board. All major projects and investments must undergo the Single Assurance Framework (SAF), meaning all projects are reviewed to ensure that they meet Corporate aims and objectives, before commencing (corporate aims include reducing emissions). The SAF follows a flexible and proportionate 'single pot' approach where the West Midlands Combined Authority is the accountable body, providing an independent view of risk and appraisal. The WMCA continues to lobby central government for further funding and power for climate action, as detailed elsewhere.\nIn 2024, the WMCA was awarded £6m by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero for a two-year Local Net Zero Accelerator programme to investigate how to fund net zero projects using a range of blended funding sources. The programme is exploring options for leveraging funding and finance from a range of investors looking for diverse outcomes, such as improved health outcomes from retrofitted homes. This is similar to the Local Investment in Natural Capital work, which received £1million from Defra to begin to create an investable projects and interested investors for nature projects. We are working with Anthesis as part of a programme to explore the potential of 'Authority Based Insetting'. This is to encourage private investment into projects that have a carbon/ environment benefit within the West Midlands region, rather than spending this investment elsewhere, including internationally.

Through the annual carbon budgeting process, Zero Carbon Whitby Projects are prioritized and included in the capital budget. 

In 2024 the Town has received several provincial and federal grants to support our climate goals including $25,000,000 for the new Whitby Sports Complex from the Green and Inclusive Community Buildings Program. As a result of this funding the Whitby Sports Complex will be will be LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) Gold and CaGBC Zero Carbon Building Design certified. 

In support of Zero Carbon Whitby, a Zero Carbon Revolving Reserve Fund (ZCRRF) was established in September 2022 to facilitate the implementation of the zero carbon projects. The ZCRRF provides a way to help pay for zero carbon retrofits, pilot projects and to fund incremental retrofit project costs of zero carbon options. Operational savings from 2024 Zero Carbon projects will be directed into the fund to help pay for future projects. The current uncommitted balance in the ZCRRF is approximately $136,000.

H&F supports decarbonisation and climate action projects with a variety of financial mechanisms, including allocating funding from internal budgets and applying for national and regional funds and grants. Other sources of funding for climate action include:

H&F Green Investment: 
https://www.abundanceinvestment.com/council/hammersmith-and-fulham
In 2023, H&F Council launched H&F Green Investment - a £5 million investment offer to support local climate and ecological projects. The fund raised £1.7 million in 2024 and supports projects to cut emissions, improve the local environment and help residents to adapt to climate change impacts.

Carbon Offset Fund:
https://www.lbhf.gov.uk/planning/climate-change-and-planning/carbon-offsetting-payments-guidance-developers-0 
Hammersmith & Fulham Council supports decarbonisation by collecting carbon offset payments. Carbon offsetting is a planning requirement under Section 106 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 and allows developers to meet local climate policies when it's not possible to reduce all carbon emissions on-site. Major new developments are expected to get as close as possible to net zero-carbon through on-site measures, meeting the GLA's and London Plan's carbon reduction targets. Where it is clearly demonstrated that net-zero carbon cannot be fully achieved on site, the shortfall is provided through a cash in lieu contribution to H&F's Carbon Offset Fund. This fund is ring-fenced for projects delivering a measurable carbon reduction in H&F. From 1 July 2025, developers of major projects in Hammersmith & Fulham are encouraged to use the Local Carbon Pricing Mechanism to calculate carbon offset payments.

Social Value:
https://democracy.lbhf.gov.uk/documents/s123113/Appendix%201%20-%20Sourcing%20Strategy%202022-2026.pdf
Added social value is a key component of H&F Council's Sourcing Strategy and there is a mandatory requirement for contracts over £100,000 to incorporate added value of 20%. These contributions from suppliers have been used to support climate projects, such as ecology and adaptation initiatives in H&F schools.

The tax applies to the seven-county Twin Cities metropolitan area, and allows us to fund many of our climate related transportation and transit projects.

The CCR pension fund is part of the Local Government Pension Fund and managed by Rhondda Cynon Taf Council.: The Pensions Committee's Climate Change Investment Policy outlined a number of key actions for the Fund in working towards a reduction of the Fund's exposure to Environmental risks. A key action was to facilitate the movement of “passive” investments to Investment Funds tracking low carbon indices. This Pension Fund has made substantial progress with this action with two significant investments, in February 2020 and July 2021, being made in the BlackRock Low Carbon Equity Tracker Fund. This Pension Fund's holding in the Low Carbon Fund was 616 million as at 31 March 2022 which represented 23% of the total value of the Pension Fund at this date. A significant proportion of the Pension Fund's investments are held in pooled Wales Pension Partnership (WPP) products. Pooling Investment resources through the WPP has enabled the 8 Welsh Local Government Pension Scheme (LGPS) Funds to appoint a Voting and Engagement provider. Although this activity will cover the full range of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) initiatives Environmental Risks, including those presented by carbon emissions, will feature prominently in the engagement activity undertaken. For 3 of the WPP Equity sub-funds the Investment Manager, Russell Investments, has introduced a “decarbonisation overlay” which has the target of reducing the carbon intensity of the sub-fund by 25% compared to the sub-funds benchmark.

Institutional capacity and the local government's commitment to sustainable budget management also play a key role in facilitating climate investment.\n\nTo fully leverage climate investment, Sumbawa Regency requires external support in several areas, including climate financing from national and international institutions, technology transfer for renewable energy, capacity building for human resources and institutional strengthening in green financial planning, and technical assistance in monitoring, evaluation, and reporting of climate action outcomes. column15: Social forestry is a strategy that aims to integrate ecological, economic, and social aspects in forest management. By empowering local communities, social forestry shifts the focus from centralized forest management to active community participation. This approach not only supports nature conservation but also improves social welfare and economic empowerment. The success of social forestry can create synergy between nature conservation and sustainable economic development, giving local communities the right to manage and utilize forest resources in their areas.\nThe Indonesian government has allocated approximately 12.7 million hectares of forest areas to communities through social forestry, as stipulated in the Minister of Environment and Forestry Regulation (PermenLHK) Number 9/MENLHK/2021 concerning Social Forestry Management. This concept provides incentives for communities to maintain forest sustainability while improving their well-being.

The development of a social forestry-based Integrated Area Development (IAD) Master Plan is based on a comprehensive and structured framework. The main steps in developing this master plan include:
1. Situation Analysis. Involves an in-depth analysis of the ecological, social, and economic conditions in the focus area. A thorough understanding of local uniqueness and challenges forms the basis for strategic planning.
2. Active Stakeholder Participation. Policy analysis by stakeholders to understand all aspects of formal policies and local wisdom. Involve all stakeholders, such as local communities, regional governments, non-governmental organizations, and the private sector, in the decision-making process conducted in a series of workshops for the development of the master plan document. This active participation ensures fair representation and sustainable implementation.
3. Zoning and Clustering for Commodity Development. Establish clear zoning and clustering for conservation (protection), natural resource utilization, and community economic development activities. Resource management must adhere to sustainability principles to avoid environmental degradation.
4. Development of capacity-building, business, and commodity development programs. Build the capacity of local communities in forest management, including through training programs, mentoring, assistance, and hands-on practice. This program is not only related to the technical aspects of forest management and business development, but also includes an understanding of community rights and responsibilities that are integrated with the programs, activities and financing of the parties.

The Climate Village Program (ProKlim) is a national program from the Ministry of Environment and Forestry (KLHK) to encourage community action at the village/gampong/kelurahan level in addressing climate change.

Main Objectives of ProKlim Villages
1. Increase community resilience
Gampongs are better prepared to face the impacts of climate change, such as tidal flooding, drought, crop failure, or climate-related diseases.

2. Reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions
Through concrete actions at the local level, such as 3R waste management, reforestation, use of renewable energy, and energy efficiency.

3. Encourage active community participation
Empower residents, farmer groups, women's groups, youth, schools, and village leaders to participate in climate action.

4. Integrate local wisdom with environmentally friendly technologies
Use traditional methods (e.g., mangrove planting, infiltration wells) combined with new innovations (biogas, rooftop solar power plants).

5. Improving community welfare
Climate action is linked to local economic opportunities: waste banks become savings, mangrove products for ecotourism, and organic waste is used for fertilizer/animal feed.

6. Supporting national climate targets
Villages' direct contribution to achieving Indonesia's NDC (emission reduction and climate change adaptation).

Several factors support climate-related investment and financial planning in Athienou Municipality. At the national level, Cyprus' policies, including the National Energy and Climate Plan and the National Waste Management Strategy, provide a framework that enables municipalities to align local projects with national priorities and access relevant funding streams.
Access to European funding instruments is a key driver, with opportunities through LIFE, Horizon Europe, the Cohesion Fund, and the Recovery and Resilience Facility. Athienou has already gained experience through participation in EU-funded initiatives such as “SEE THE SEA,” which strengthen capacity to apply for and implement funded projects.
Partnerships with national ministries and the Larnaca District Administration also support financial planning by providing technical guidance, co-financing opportunities, and integration of municipal projects into larger regional or national programs.
At the local level, Athienou has demonstrated commitment through energy efficiency measures (LED street lighting, photovoltaic installations), waste management improvements, and green space development. These actions provide evidence of successful implementation and help to build confidence among potential funders and investors.
Finally, strong community engagement is an important enabling factor. Active involvement of residents, schools, NGOs, and vulnerable groups increases the social acceptance of climate projects and enhances their long-term sustainability, making them more attractive for external investment.
Together, these factors create an enabling environment for Athienou to attract and manage climate-related financing, despite the challenges of being a small municipality with limited internal resources.

The City Development Investment Program (CDIP) is a comprehensive framework designed to guide the city's growth and development over a medium to long-term horizon. It focuses on strategic investments that aim to enhance the city's infrastructure, economic competitiveness, social services, and environmental sustainability. The program identifies priority sectors such as agriculture, industry, tourism, trade, and public utilities, ensuring that development initiatives are aligned with the city's vision of becoming a dynamic and inclusive urban center.

The CDIP is formulated through a participatory and consultative process involving multiple stakeholders to ensure that the program reflects the community's needs and development priorities. 

The process typically includes Data Collection and Situation Analysis, Stakeholder Consultations, Setting Development Goals and Priorities, Project Identification and Investment Programming, Drafting and Validation, and Approval and Implementation. 

Through this inclusive and evidence-based approach, the CDIP serves as a roadmap to foster sustainable and inclusive growth, improve public services and infrastructure, promote investment, and enhance the overall quality of life for Butuan's residents.

The Annual Investment Program (AIP) is an LGU's one-year work and financial plan, detailing priority Programs, Projects, and Activities (PPAs) across sectors such as economic services, social services, and general public services. It translates broader development strategies from LGU plans into actionable, budget-aligned initiatives.
 
The steps for AIP consist of Development Planning, PPA Drafting and Formulation Process, Stakeholder Involvement, Council Review, AIP Approval, Budget Allocation, Implementation & Oversight, and Adjustments.
